newsitem.title: TAIWAN: INTERVIEW-Taiwan notebook PC maker to make debut.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Taiwan notebook PC maker to make debut.

text.p: Having built one of Taiwan's top global high-technology brands, notebook computer maker Twinhead International Corp is banking on a dazzling stock market debut -- and a tripling of sales by 2001.
Twinhead, one of Taiwan's top five notebook makers, makes its stock exchange entry on Monday at a time of hot profits and surging growth in Taiwan's new bedrock sector, electronics.
"We believe Taiwan's notebook computer makers will enjoy high 30-35 percent annual compound growth in coming years," Twinhead president I.J. Lee told Reuters on Thursday.
"We have a goal to reach sales revenue of T$50 billion (US$1.74 billion) in 2001," Lee said in an interview.
At that rate, Taiwan's notebook growth would outstrip worldwide growth by a wide margin. Lee said notebook computer production is growing 20-25 percent a year.
Twinhead will list with an underwriting price of T$67.5 (US$2.35) per share. The grey market price had surged to T$100.5 (US$3.5) on Wednesday, suggesting an auspicious debut.
Analysts said they expected Twinhead to rise sharply.
"As electronics firms enter their hot-sale season in the third and fourth quarters, Twinhead no doubt can rise to above T$100 after debut," said independent analyst Michael Hung.

Twinhead had net profits of T$430 million (US$15 million) on sales of T$14.1 billion (US$491 million) in 1996, and expects to reach a 1997 net profit of T$630 million (US$22 million) on sales of T$18.5 billion (US$645 million), Lee said.
Notebooks have become the mainstay for Twinhead, whose machines have won awards from local and foreign computer magazines and competitions.
"Notebooks will remain our main focus though we're extending our investment to related peripheral production," he said. Twinhead has invested in making printers and digital cameras.
"When our sales revenues exceed T$50 billion, we will set up our own sales channels and further expand to upstream and downstream products," Lee said.

Notebook computers, which need intense integration of optoelectronics, electronics, graphics and heat and power management, have a voracious appetite for long-term investment in design and research and development, Lee said.
Lee said Twinhead has an innovative edge due to its team of designers, who each have seven years or more of experience.
Research and development soaks up 3.5 percent of revenues.
Taiwan already is the world's notebook king. The island made 3.77 million in 1996, up 46 percent from 1995, according to the semi-official Institute for Information Industry.
The institute estimated Taiwan can turn out 4.8 million notebook computers in 1997, up 27 percent from 1996.
Twinhead expects to produce 430,000 notebook computers in 1997, up from 292,000 in 1996, Lee said.
With completion of a new plant in June, the firm will be able to turn out 600,000-700,000 units in 1998, Lee said.

Twinhead adopt what Lee called a "6-3-1" sales strategy -- 60 percent of sales going to original equipment manufacturing (OEM), 30 percent to its own brand and 10 percent to original design manufacturing, marketing Twinhead designs under other brands.
"The 6-3-1 strategy is to avoid risks and try to secure our clients," Lee said.
The firm has four major OEM clients -- one in Japan and three in the United States -- and a possible newcomer in Europe, Lee said. Citing confidentiality pacts, he would not name them.
Some 40 percent of Twinhead's sales go to the United States, 30 percent to Japan, 15 percent to Europe, 10 percent to Taiwan and five percent to mainland China, Lee said.
Twinhead is the top notebook brand in the Taiwan market, holding a 38 percent share, and is number two in China.
